attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you brainstorm the functions that might be added to set up the the Inventory menu?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

N/A 


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the structure of Red Belt Build activities differ from previous belts in IMPACT?

❓ What functions might be used to set up the 3 levels and multiple waves, throughout the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja how the structure of Red Belt will differ from prior belts in IMPACT. In Red Belt, multiple Build activities across the level will be used to construct a larger, complex project based on a given theme (instead of multiple, individual projects). The starter code for each successive Build activity will be populated with code from the previous Build activity. At the end of the level, the ninja will have an opportunity to create their own complex project to add to their Red Belt portfolio, using theme-specific concepts applied throughout the Build activities.

💡 If a ninja is unfamiliar with a tower defense style of game, guide them through the basic features. The user will set up towers throughout the game area. Once towers have been placed, the wave will begin where enemies will move across the screen. The towers will send projectiles towards the enemies. The user’s score increases for each enemy destroyed, but decreases if there are enemies that are able to progress through the path at the end of each wave. Each wave gets progressively faster and more challenging as more enemies appear on screen.

💡 Prompt the ninja to brainstorm specific functions that might be needed to set up the the Inventory menu. Encourage the ninja to write down ideas as pseudocode to think through the sequence and the logic of the tower defense code.
steps.instructions:
This is the third of 4 Build activities where you will create a tower defense project!


Notice that the code from the Build 2 activity has already been added into the JavaScript editor.


In the third Build activity, you will increase the complexity of the game experience and enhance the User Interface (UI) by designing an interactive Inventory menu for the user to access Tower sprites through. The user will be able to open and close the username, then select a Tower sprite based on its price and power functionality.


What functions might be used to set up the Inventory menu?

steps.hints: ❓Did you replace the 0 in callScene with 2, 3, or 4 so that you can bypass the start screen to more easily test the Inventory menu in the following steps?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you highlight the entire controller event, then press Ctrl + / to comment it out?

❓ What number might be passed to the callScene function to easily test one of the game levels?

❓ How might an Inventory menu supplement the A button functionality? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the ninja is unfamiliar, guide the ninja in the process of highlighting the entire controller event to comment it out. Point out where their cursor should be and how to hold down the left mouse button to highlight an entire section. Once highlighted, demonstrate how Ctrl + / can be used to comment out the section, then uncomment it when pressed again.

💡 In this activity, the ninja will build an Inventory menu, where they can use money earned from destroying Enemy sprites to buy Tower sprites of different sizes (and power capability). An Inventory is a great way to incorporate user choice into a project to improve the user’s experience.
steps.instructions:
Prepare the project for the creation and testing of an Inventory menu.


Deactivate the A button pressed functionality temporarily by highlighting the lines of code that make up the controller.A.onEvent and using Ctrl + / to comment out the entire section of code. 


Under // run game, update the argument passed to callScene to the sceneNum parameter of one of the game levels, so the inventory menu can be more easily tested.


Click ▶ to test the A button to ensure it no longer places Tower sprites on the sandTile assets on the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓Did you create 2 separate variables for the inventory menu: one that creates the image, and one that creates a sprite using that image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the image.create function do? What is it being used for?

❓ What keyword should be used to declare an inventoryRect image variable, and an inventory sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The image.create function creates a new, transparent image on screen (this is why the image does not appear on screen yet). It takes 2 parameters: width and height of the shape in pixels. The function will create the background shape for the inventory menu.

💡 Remind the ninja to use the keyword let to declare the inventoryRect image variable and inventory sprite. Then, they can use the code documentation tool for guidance when adding argument values inside the parentheses.
steps.instructions:
Set up the code to create an inventory menu in the project!


First, add an Inventory sprite kind. Then, under // game functions, define a callInventory function with 1 boolean parameter: “open”. 


Inside the function definition, add a // create rectangle comment, then set the variable inventoryRect to an empty rectangle shape. In Images, drag out [create image width (width) height (height)]. The image.create function creates a transparent image and takes 2 parameters: a width, and a height. 


Create a rectangle with a width of 65 and a height of 120. Then, create an inventory sprite that uses inventoryRect as the image and Inventory as the sprite kind.

steps.hints: ❓Did you position the Inventory menu rectangle on the right side of the screen, like this:
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How should the fill and drawRect functions be formatted, so that they update the inventoryRect image?

❓ How do the x and y parameters of the drawRect function affect where the rectangle will be drawn?

❓ Which variable should be used to position the Inventory menu?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to type the name of the inventoryRect variable followed by a dot operator. They can then either select the function names from the code completion tool or type them out. Remind the ninja to type a pair of parentheses after the function name, then use the code documentation tool for help with adding arguments inside.

💡 The drawRect function positions the rectangle shape relative to the image created, not the screen position. In this example, the drawRect function is being used to draw an outline for the Inventory menu, so 0, 0 is used so that the white outline is placed directly on top of the blue rectangle.

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice that the an image’s position cannot be set using the setPosition function; a sprite is required. The ninja should use the inventory sprite to set the position of the Inventory menu on screen.
steps.instructions:
Stylize and position the Inventory menu so it is visible on screen!


Inside the callInventory function definition, use the fill function with the inventoryRect variable to fill the empty shape with dark blue (8). 


Under // run game, call the callInventory function, passing the argument true to view the Inventory rectangle on screen.


Then, use the drawRect function to draw a thin white outline (1) around the rectangle shape. Use 0 as the x and y arguments, then use the guidance in the documentation pop up to set the remaining parameters so the rectangle shape appears on the border of the Inventory menu correctly.


Then, set the position of the Inventory menu sprite so it appears on the right side, up against the right edge of the screen.


Click ▶ to test the position and color of the rectangle and border, and edit the parameters until it looks as expected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the position of the text sprite relative to the screen, and the divider line position relative to the rectangle shape?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the drawLine function do? How do the parameter values affect its appearance?

❓ How do the x and y parameters of the textsprite.create and drawLine function differ?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The drawLine function draws a line on an image. It takes 5 parameters: x0, y0, x1, y1, c. Encourage the ninja to use the code documentation tool typing out their code. The x0 and y0 parameters set the starting x and y-positions of the line (relative to the image on which the line is being drawn). The x1 and y1 parameters set the ending x and y-positions of the line (relative to the image on which the line is being drawn). The c parameter sets the color of the drawn line.


💡 Guide the ninja in identifying which arguments to pass to the createTextSprite and drawLine functions, explaining how the x and y arguments will differ between the two. The textsprite.create function positions the text relative to the entire screen, whereas the drawLine function draws a line relative to the rectangle image shape, similar to the drawRect function from the previous step.
steps.instructions:
Add a title to the Inventory menu.


Inside the callInventory function definition, call the createTextSprite function to display the word “Inventory” in white (1) across the top of the Inventory menu. Remember that hovering over the function shows all of the possible parameters:


Then use the drawLine function with the inventoryRect variable to draw a divider line underneath the text sprite, in the same color as the border. 


Click ▶ to test the position and color of the text and divider line, and edit the parameters until it looks as expected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you align the TowerImage sprite and the cost text on the Inventory menu, like this:
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Where can the names of the 3 different sized Tower image assets be found?

❓ Where might the TowerImage sprites and each tower’s cost be placed in the Inventory menu?

❓ What function should be used to convert the elements in the towerCosts array into strings that can be displayed on screen?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ninja can use My Assets to locate the names of the 3 different sized Tower image assets.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider what values are needed to properly space out the y-positions of each TowerImage sprite and their costs. The setPosition functions will place sprites relative to the entire screen, not just the rectangle image. The spacing between sprites should be calculated first, which should be multiplied by the loop’s counter variable i inside parentheses. Then, the initial y-position (or the yOffset) of the first TowerImage sprite should be added to the equation. The code might look like: 

towerSprite.setPosition(110, 32 + (i * 22))

💡 Remind the ninja to use the convertToText function to convert the number elements in the towerCosts array into string values that can be displayed on screen.
steps.instructions:
Create different Tower sprite options to be displayed on the Inventory.

 

Create a TowerImage sprite kind. After the code that sets up the Sprite Kind, add an // inventory initialization comment, then declare a towerImages array underneath that contains the 3 different sized Tower image asset names, in order from small to large. Then declare a towerCosts array containing the cost of the 3 different sized Tower sprites: 100, 200, and 300.

 

Inside the callInventory function definition, add a // create tower inventory comment. Use a for loop to create local TowerImage sprites, setting their images to elements inside the towerImages array. Use the loop’s counter variable to select and position the image on the top left side of the Inventory menu. Set the TowerImage sprites’ z-position so they appear in front of the rectangle image.

 

Then, add a  // display tower cost comment, and use another for loop to display the cost of the 3 different Tower sprites, using the createTextSprite function to display the costs next to the TowerImage sprites. Use the loop’s counter variable to select and position the value from the towerCost array. Make sure to use a different counter variable name!

 

Click ▶ to test the positions of the Tower images and costs, and edit the parameters until they look as expected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you position the text that displays the game wave and money variables on the Inventory menu, like this:
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution: 


Ask the ninja:

❓ What keyboard shortcut can be used to easily navigate the code in the project?

❓ Where might the gameWaveCount and money text sprites be placed, so that they appear underneath the TowerImage sprites and costs in the Inventory menu?

❓ What function should be used to convert the elements in the towerCosts array into strings that can be displayed on screen?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to use Ctrl + F to search for function names in the code to access them easily, especially as they are updating code in multiple parts of the editor at once.

💡 Prompt the ninja to continuously test out the placement and appearance of the gameWaveCount and money variables in the Inventory variables, ensuring that they are visible and spaced out correctly within the rectangular shape. Encourage the ninja to tinker with the position of the TowerImage sprites and their costs as needed, to ensure the alignment of all pieces. The Inventory menu is a big part of the User Interface (UI) for the tower defense project, so it’s important that it looks clean and is intuitive for the user!

💡 Remind the ninja to use the convertToText function to convert the gameWaveCount and money number variables into string values that can be displayed on screen.
steps.instructions:
Show the wave count and amount of money remaining on the Inventory menu.

 

Inside the callInventory function definition, below the for loops, add a // show wave and money UI comment. Use a createTextSprite function to display the gameWaveCount variable and the waveIcon image asset below the Tower images on the Inventory menu. Because the gameWaveCount variable does not increase until the wave starts, add 1 to the variable so the Inventory menu displays the correct wave number.

 

Then, cut the createTextSprite function used to display the money variable from the createScreenText function, and paste it into the callInventory function definition, updating the position so it appears below the wave count.

 

Inside the initializeLevel function definition, update the money variable to 300 or more, so the player has more money to spend on Towers at the beginning of the game.

 

Click ▶ to test the positions of the game wave and money variables, and edit the parameters until they look as expected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you remove the callInventory function from under // run game so the function is only called when the B button is pressed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use Ctrl + F to search for function names in the code to access them easily, especially as they are updating code in multiple parts of the editor at once.

💡 Walk through the logic of the B button pressed event with the ninja. If the B button is pressed, and inventoryOpen is true, the inventoryOpen variable will be set to false and the Inventory menu will not open. If the B button is pressed and inventoryOpen is false, the variable will be set to true and the Inventory menu will open. This logic ensures that the Inventory menu can only be open if it is not currently displayed on screen.
steps.instructions:
Code the B button to open the Inventory menu.

 

Under // inventory initialization add an inventoryOpen variable set to false.

 

Add an // inventory events comment at the bottom of the editor, with code for a B button pressed event underneath. Use a conditional that sets the inventoryOpen variable to false if it returns true, else sets it to true.

 

Then, cut the callInventory function call from under // run game and paste it into the B button pressed event, replacing true with the inventoryOpen variable.

steps.hints: ❓Did you destroy all of the sprites used to create the Inventory menu on the screen, then call the createScreenText function to place the lives text sprite on screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Does the Inventory menu open and close each time the B button is pressed, as expected?

❓ Did you use the open function parameter to set when the Inventory menu is opened and closed?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to test out pressing the B button multiple times to ensure that it opens and closes as expected.

💡 Remind the ninja to use the open function parameter in the if/ else if conditional inside the callInventory function, not the inventoryOpen variable.
steps.instructions:
Close the Inventory menu when the B button is pressed again.

 

Inside the callInventory function definition, add a conditional checking for the open Boolean parameter to be true. Inside the conditional, add a // open inventory menu comment, then cut and paste all of the code currently in the function inside.

 

Add an else if condition that checks for the open Boolean parameter to be false.Add a // close inventory menu comment, then use 3 destroyAllSpritesOfKind functions to remove the ScreenText, Inventory, and TowerImage sprites from the screen. Then, call the createScreenText function to make the lives variable text reappear on screen.

 

Click ▶ to test opening and closing the Inventory menu with the B button.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use cursor.image.equals to check which asset the Cursor sprite is set to?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ When is the Cursor sprite’s image set to the squareCursor asset? When is it set to the arrowCursor asset?

❓ Why is it important to update the Cursor sprite’s image as it interacts with different sprite kinds in the project?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Cursor sprite overlaps a TowerImage sprite in the Inventory menu, its image will be set to the squareCursor asset. When it overlaps an Inventory sprite (the Inventory menu image), its image will be reset to the arrowCursor asset. The Cursor sprite’s image will also be reset to the arrowCursor asset when the Inventory menu is closed.

💡 Ask the ninja to consider how they know something is clickable (or interactable) when navigating a website. When something is clickable, the cursor changes a pointer finger.

💡 Prompt the ninja to test out pressing the B button multiple times, then using the direction buttons to move the Cursor sprite to overlap different types of sprites, to ensure that the Cursor sprite’s image updates correctly.
steps.instructions:
Change the cursor image if it is overlapping with a TowerImage sprite on the Inventory menu.

 

Under // game play events, use an onOverlap event to change the Cursor image to the squareCursor asset when it overlaps a TowerImage sprite. Use another onOverlap event to change the Cursor back to the arrowCursor asset when it overlaps an Inventory sprite.

 

In the callInventory function definition, inside the else if condition that runs when the Inventory menu is being closed, add a nested conditional that changes the Cursor image back to the arrowCursor asset if it is set to the squareCursor asset when the B button is pressed.

 

Click ▶ to test how the Cursor image changes when it overlaps different parts of the Inventory menu.

steps.hints: ❓Did you call the callInventory function with the inventoryOpen parameter set to false to close the Inventory menu after a Tower image has been selected?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the A button is pressed while the Cursor sprite is overlapping a TowerImage sprite?

❓ What happens to the Inventory menu after a TowerImage sprite is selected?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the A button is pressed while the Cursor sprite is overlapping a TowerImage sprite, the Cursor sprite’s image will be set to the selected TowerImage sprite’s image, and the Inventory menu will be closed. The user will then be able to position the TowerImage sprite on the tilemap.

💡 Remind the ninja to use the sprite and otherSprite variables from the overlap event to update the Cursor sprite’s image.
steps.instructions:
Select a Tower from the Inventory menu!

 

Under // inventory initialization add a holdingTower variable set to false.

 

Inside the Cursor/TowerImage overlap event, add a conditional that checks if the A button is being pressed. Inside, use the setImage function to set the Cursor image to that of the TowerImage being overlapped, using the sprite and otherSprite variables from the overlap event.

 

Set the holdingTower variable to true and the inventoryOpen variable to false, then call the callInventory function, passing inventoryOpen as the parameter.

 

Click ▶ to test how the Cursor image changes when using the A button to select one of the 3 Tower image assets.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use cursor.image.equals to check for all 3 TowerImage asset sizes, separated by || operators?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Are you able to select and place different types of TowerImage sprites, as expected?  

❓ What symbols should be used to check that a sandTile is at the Cursor sprite’s center and that the Cursor sprite’s image is set to one of the TowerImage sprite images?

❓ Why is the Cursor sprite’s image reset, once the TowerImage sprite is placed on the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the Inventory menu and positioning lots of different towers at this step. The money variable will be added back in in the next step, which will limit the ability to test this functionality.

💡 Prompt the ninja to use an && operator, and multiple || operators with the code that checks for the 3 TowerImage sprite images inside parentheses, like this: 


if (cursor.tileKindAt(TileDirection.Center, assets.tile`sandTile`) && (cursor.image.equals(assets.image`smallTowerImage`) || cursor.image.equals(assets.image`medTowerImage`) || cursor.image.equals(assets.image`largeTowerImage`))) {...}


💡 To create a consistent User Interface (UI), it’s important that the cursor matches the action being taken from the user. There are 3 different images (arrowCursor, squareCursor, and the 3 tower images) that tell the user they can perform different actions, which must be updated to reflect what’s happening in the project.
steps.instructions:
Place the selected Tower on the tilemap.


Restore the A button pressed functionality by highlighting the code and using Ctrl + / again to remove the code comments. 


Delete the code that decreases the money variable by 100 and updates the on-screen text. This will be updated in a later step.


In the if condition, there are 2 conditions; delete the code that checks if the money variable is greater than or equal to 100. Add code that checks for each of the 3 sizes of TowerImage assets instead. Use OR operators to check for all 3 TowerImage assets. Surround the code with parentheses so the condition checks for the sandTile tile asset AND one of the 3 TowerImage assets. 


Use cursor.image in the code that creates the towerClone sprite. Then, add code in the conditional to change the Cursor’s image back to the arrowCursor image asset, and change the holdingTower variable back to false.


Click ▶ to test the Tower placement functionality with all 3 of the Tower size options.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the distance parameter for each getSpritesWithin function and the towerVelocity value for all 3 of the TowerImage size options, so the small Tower has the smallest range and slowest Projectile speed, and the large Tower has the largest range and fastest Projectile speed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the distance parameter for each getSpritesWithin function and the towerVelocity value for all 3 of the TowerImage size options be set to?

❓ What happens now when different TowerImage size options are placed on the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use Ctrl + F to search for function names in the code to access them easily.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider how far each Tower sprite should be able to send a Projectile from, and how quickly it should move across the tilemap. Encourage the ninja to test out a variety of values to differentiate the behaviors of each Tower sprite.
steps.instructions:
Update the Tower sprite’s range and projectile velocity based on its size.


Inside the onSpriteKindUpdateInterval function, inside the conditional that checks if gameWave is true, add a // launch projectile comment before the nested condition that checks if target is true.


Above // launch projectile, add a // check image and set tower velocity comment and add a nested conditional. Create 2 else if conditions, then use the equals function to check if the tower sprite image is equal to one of the 3 possible TowerImage assets in the 3 conditions. 


Cut the existing code that sets the target and towerVelocity and paste it inside all 3 of the new conditional statements.


Update the distance parameter for each getSpritesWithin function so the smallest Tower has the smallest range and the largest Tower has the largest. Then update the towerVelocity values so the smallest Tower has a slower speed and the largest Tower has the fastest.


Click ▶ to test the range and projectile velocity of the different sized Tower sprites.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use otherSprite.image.equals to check for 1 of the 3 possible TowerImage options, with an && operator to also check if there is enough money available to select that Tower sprite without the money variable going below 0?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Which function variable should be used to access the image of the TowerImage sprite being overlapped?

❓ What value of the money variable should be checked for inside the if/else if/else if conditions?

❓ What happens when the user tries to select a Tower sprite, if they do not have enough money to purchase it? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ninja should use the otherSprite variable to access the image of the TowerImage sprite being overlapped in the 3 conditions.

💡 Prompt the ninja to refer back to the values stored in the towerCosts array to find the cost of each Tower sprite.

💡 Now, the user will only be able to select a TowerImage sprite from the Inventory menu if they have enough money to cover its cost. If so, the TowerImage  sprite’s cost will be deducted from the money variable when selected from the Inventory menu.
steps.instructions:
Deduct different amounts of money based on the Tower size selected from the Inventory menu.


Inside the Cursor/TowerImage overlap event, add a nested conditional inside the conditional that checks if the A button is pressed, above the other code already inside it. Create 2 else if conditions. For each condition, use the equals function to check for one of the 3 possible TowerImage assets.


Then, cut the setImage code and paste it inside all 3 of the new conditional statements.


Notice that each tower has a different cost! For each condition, use an AND operator to also check if the money variable is greater than or equal to the cost of the Tower sprite. Then, inside each conditional, subtract the cost of the Tower sprite from the money variable inside the conditional statement.


Click ▶ to test that a Tower sprite can only be selected if there is enough money available, and that the correct amount of money is deducted when it is selected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you create a new conditional around the existing code inside both the A and B button pressed events, that checks for levelStarted to be true before running the code inside?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the levelStarted variable affect the user’s button capability?

❓ Can the Inventory menu be opened and closed at the correct points throughout the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to play through the project thoroughly to ensure everything is working properly. Prompt the ninja to tinker with values and explore how the Boolean variables keep track of game conditions. Then, see if the ninja can make it through all 10 waves of each level!
steps.instructions:
Prevent the Inventory menu from showing before the game begins, or during a game wave.


Under // game initialization add a levelStarted variable set to false.


Inside the initializeLevel function definition, set levelStarted to true. 


Inside the A button pressed event, add a conditional around the existing code that checks if levelStarted is true before running the code that checks for the tile and image assets to place a Tower sprite.


Inside the B button pressed event, add a conditional around the existing code that checks if the inventoryOpen variable is true. Set the conditional to check if levelStarted is true, then use AND operators to also check that gameWave and holdingTower are false, so that the Inventory menu does not open at the wrong time.


Under // run game, update the argument passed to callScene to 0. Then, thoroughly test the new Inventory menu and Tower size features to ensure they all work as expected on each level of the game.

subgroups.introduction: Continue building a Tower Defense project that includes an Inventory menu with different sized towers to choose from! Including a variety of defense towers with different costs will increase the complexity and the user strategy required to improve the overall game experience!

validationItems.text: Use a function with a Boolean parameter to create an Inventory menu that is drawn on screen.
Create an array of Tower sprite images and costs, then use those arrays to display that data on the Inventory menu.
Display the wave count and money variables on the Inventory menu.
Open and close the Inventory menu with the B button.
Change the cursor image if it is overlapping a TowerImage sprite on the Inventory menu, then change it back when it is not.
Change the cursor image to a TowerImage sprite when selected.
Place the selected TowerImage sprite clone on the tilemap.
Change the Tower sprite’s range and Projectile velocity based on its size.
Prevent the Inventory menu from opening before the game begins or during a game wave.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Red Belt! In this level, you’ll apply your previous learning by creating a complex tower defense project in JavaScript across 4 different Build activities. There is no pre-assessment Quest activity for this level, so click “Start Level” to begin! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2

badges.title: Tower Power!
badges.description: Create a complex tower defense project in JavaScript using sprite and tile utility extensions, and a detailed Inventory menu.
